summary: Defines a Sieve extension for matching against externally stored lists, so allow lists, block lists and distribution lists do not have to be written into the script. Membership changes then need no script update. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of copying names into a rule over and over, the mail filter checks a separate list that can be changed any time.

questions: what is sieve externally stored lists
how do i use external lists in sieve
can sieve scripts reference address books
subtitle: Reference externally managed lists in email filter rules without rewriting the script.

tldr.problem: Sieve email filter scripts must hard-code list members, requiring script updates whenever membership changes. This makes whitelists, blacklists, and distribution lists cumbersome to maintain.
tldr.mechanism: The extlists extension adds a :list match type to Sieve tests and a :list argument to the redirect action, so scripts can reference externally stored lists (LDAP, ACAP, CardDAV, databases) by URI instead of embedding member data.
tldr.outcome: Users can manage list membership through directory systems, and scripts stay stable. Changes to lists take effect immediately without script updates.

today: RFC 6134 is a Proposed Standard and remains in effect. The extension is implemented by several mail servers and Sieve interpreter libraries, enabling users to maintain whitelists, blacklists, and distribution lists in external directories without script updates.

sections.title: Why External Lists Matter
sections.content:
The Sieve email filtering language (RFC 5228) can implement whitelists, blacklists and distribution lists, but only by writing member names directly into the script. When list membership changes—adding or removing an address—the script must be rewritten and re-uploaded to the mail server. This is tedious and error-prone.

This RFC defines an extension, called extlists, that lets Sieve scripts query lists stored externally: in LDAP directories, ACAP servers, CardDAV address books, or databases. The script references the list by a URI; the mail server handles the lookup. Users can now manage lists in one place—a directory, an address book—and Sieve scripts adapt immediately without changing.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing names into the rule itself, Sieve now asks an external list: Is this person on the list? If yes, apply the rule. When you add or remove a name from the list, the rule works correctly right away.

sections.title: The :list Match Type
sections.content:
Sieve tests like address, envelope, and header normally match values against hard-coded strings. The new :list match type changes that: instead of a list of values to match against, you provide a list of external list names. The test queries those lists and returns true if any value matches any member.

For example, address :list "from" ":addrbook:default" checks whether the From address belongs to the user's default address book. If it does, the test succeeds. The Sieve engine either retrieves the list itself or asks the list provider (like an LDAP server) to check membership. Not all list systems work the same way—some allow the server to download the whole list, others only support membership queries—so the implementation handles the mechanics transparently.

When using Variables (RFC 5229), the matched member value is stored in the variable ${0}, so the script can reference what it matched.
sections.eli5: Instead of checking is this person in alice, bob, carol?, you ask is this person in the list called my-friends? and the server finds out by asking the list server.

sections.title: Naming External Lists
sections.content:
External lists are identified by Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs)—the same format as web URLs. Implementations can use LDAP URIs like ldap://directory.example.com/cn=vips, CardDAV paths, tag URIs, or implementation-specific formats.

For address books, RFC 6134 defines a special URN (Uniform Resource Name) format: urn:ietf:params:sieve:addrbook:name. The mandatory one is urn:ietf:params:sieve:addrbook:default, which refers to the user's default personal address book. Scripts can use a shorthand: :addrbook:default is equivalent to the full URN. Other address books like :addrbook:personal, :addrbook:family, or :addrbook:company may be available depending on the server.

The reserved name "default" (after URI decoding) is case-insensitive, so :addrbook:DEFAULT and :addrbook:DeFauLt refer to the same address book. Other address book names may be case-sensitive, preserving their case.
sections.eli5: External lists have names like web addresses. The most common one is your address book, which the filter can call by name: :addrbook:default means your personal contacts.

sections.title: Using External Lists with Actions
sections.content:
Beyond matching tests, Sieve scripts can also use redirect :list list-name to send a message to all members of an external list, implementing a personal distribution list. The server either enumerates the addresses from the list (if the list provider supports it) and sends the message to each one, or it asks the list provider to handle the redirection on its behalf.

This works smoothly when the list contains email addresses. Some lists, however, contain hashed values or patterns like sz*@example.com, which the Sieve engine cannot enumerate. In those cases, the list provider must take responsibility for expanding and redirecting the message. If neither the Sieve engine nor the list provider can enumerate the list, the script encounters a runtime error.
sections.eli5: Instead of listing everyone to send the message to, you say send to the members of this list. The list server figures out who to send it to automatically.

sections.title: Checking List Support
sections.content:
The valid_ext_list test lets scripts check whether the server supports a given external list before trying to use it. Calling valid_ext_list ":addrbook:default" returns true if that list exists and is accessible, false otherwise. This is useful when a script might use optional features depending on what the server offers.

At compile time, the server also validates list names: if a script references a list that does not exist or is invalid, the Sieve engine may reject the script immediately or defer the error until the script actually tries to use the list at runtime.
sections.eli5: A script can ask: does this list exist on this server? If not, it can do something else instead.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
External lists are integral to script logic, so access to them should be as protected as the script itself. If a directory or list server becomes temporarily unreachable, the Sieve engine should treat it like a script that cannot be retrieved: delay message delivery and try again later, rather than silently skipping the list.

Communication with list servers must be secure—encrypted and authenticated—at least to the same degree as script retrieval. Whether encryption is required depends on the network: a private LAN serving trusted servers may not need it, but the public Internet certainly does. Public lists may need no authentication, while private ones require it.

Because external lists directly influence script behavior, anyone who can modify a list can change how mail is filtered. This is as dangerous as modifying the script itself. List content must be protected from tampering and unauthorized access.

Querying lists can be resource-intensive. A naive implementation that downloads a large list to check membership could overload the list server or the Sieve engine. Implementations should use efficient query mechanisms when available—for instance, LDAP search filters—rather than fetching entire lists. Additionally, forwarding a message to thousands of external list members could cause a mailbomb, so servers should enforce limits on recipient counts and domains.
sections.eli5: Keep lists as safe as scripts. Bad people who can change a list can redirect mail or block important messages, so protect them. Also, be careful not to forward a message to huge lists by accident.

sections.title: Address Books Across Systems
sections.content:
Address books are used by many applications—Sieve interpreters, email clients, groupware systems—and may be stored in LDAP, local files, or cloud services. The addrbook URN parameter provides a standard way for different systems to reference them, even if the underlying storage is different.

An implementation might offer multiple address books: a personal one, a family one, a company one, and a department one. Each can be accessed via its own URN. The framework is also designed to support future extensions—for instance, a dynamic subset like urn:ietf:params:sieve:addrbook:personal?name.contains=fred could select addresses matching a pattern, though no extensions are currently defined.

Implementations are only required to support addrbook:default. Other names are optional. If a server has no concept of address books at all, it may support the default URI by having all matches fail, though this is a last resort.
sections.eli5: Different mail services store address books in different ways. This standard gives them a common name so scripts work the same everywhere.

sections.title: Practical Scenarios
sections.content:
A Sieve script using the spamtest extension can give different spam tolerance to known senders: if the From address is in the user's address book, accept higher spam scores and still deliver. Otherwise, reject more aggressively. The script does not need to list every trusted sender.

Another use: check dates against a list of company holidays. If today matches a holiday in an external list, notify the user via instant message. The list is managed once by HR; every employee's script uses the same list without modification.

A distribution list implementation: if a message arrives with a subaddress like user+mylist@example.com and the sender is in the list called mylist, redirect the message to all members of that list. The script checks the list by URI; to change the list, update the directory, not the script.

IP-based filtering: extract the IP address from the last Received header, look it up against a block list of undesirable IPs, and reject if it matches. Again, the block list is external and updatable without touching the script.
sections.eli5: A manager's mail filter can check: Is this sender in my VIP list? An HR mail filter can check: Is today a company holiday? A team lead can broadcast to a distribution list without listing everyone in the script.
